:::{.callout-note title="Overview"}
In this lecture, we focus on *perspectives* or how we can think about visualization.

We look at:

1. Recent history –-- a selective sketch
2. Important case studies –-- a discussion
3. Identify your goals –-- a tool kit
4. Think about your audience --– a tool kit

You can navigate to each in the side bar on the right.
:::

#### Linked resources {#sec-7143-w6-lectures-out-links}

In a [linked lecture in PSYC7142](../PSYC7142/part2/7142_vis-practices.qmd#sec-7142-vis-lectures), we look at *practices* or how you can work effectively to produce visualizations.

In that linked lecture, we look at how you can:

  - Ask yourself the critical questions that will help you to figure out what you need to do
  - Understand your development of visualizations as a reflective process
  - Combine your creative thinking with the Grammar of Graphics to produce visualizations
  
There is a little repetition if you compare the two lectures because I do not assume you must view the perspectives lecture to understand the practices lecture.  

::: callout-tip
In the [linked tutorial in PSYC7142](../PSYC7142/part2/visualization.qmd#sec-vis-aims), we provide in-depth explanation of development processes and code steps that you can follow-up if you want to learn more about developing and producing visualizations for discovery and communication.
:::

### Interactive lecture -- This week, we think about data visualization {#sec-7143-w6-lectures-lecture} 

You can watch the lecture videos using the playback windows shown next. The lecture is broken into four parts.

1. **Recent history –-- A reminder of why data visualization matters**
2. **Important case studies –-- What they teach us**
3. **What are our goals –-- Questions to reflect on**
4. **Think about your audience –-- An evidence based account of what works**

::: callout-tip
During the lecture, I suggest some questions you can think about. Reflecting on your responses to these questions will help you to learn.
:::

You can download the lecture slides as a .html file you can open in any browser.

The slides end with a references list but don't worry about reading what's in the references list, we give you recommended readings in @sec-7143-w6-reading.

::: callout-tip
The slides presented in the next videos can be downloaded as a web page: `data-visualisation-perspectives.html`. 

- [Lecture slides](files/data-visualisation-perspectives.html)

When you download the file, double click on it to open it in your usual web browser for viewing.
:::

Next, you can see the lecture elements. We recommend that you watch them in sequence.

1. **Recent history –-- A reminder of why data visualization matters** (~38 minutes). Lessons from recent history: I talk about why visualizations are important, in science, and in how science relates to society, by discussing recent examples of influential visualizations.

3. **What are our goals –-- Questions to reflect on** (~15 minutes). Why bother learning about visualization or investing time in doing it well? I identify questions you can ask yourself, and reflect on, in deciding whether or how to invest your time and energy in developing more effective visualizations.

## Reading {#sec-7143-w6-reading}

::: {.callout-tip title="Easy access to readings"}
All reading is accessible via the library.

- **Essential**: We expect you to be familiar with these reading. You will be assessed on this.
- **Recommended**: We highly recommend these readings. They often provide a different perspective, or explain things in a different way.
- **Optional**: Further readings for those interested.
:::

This week, the reading is optional but **Recommended**:

Franconeri, S. L., Padilla, L. M., Shah, P., Zacks, J. M., & Hullman, J. (2021). The Science of Visual Data Communication: What Works. *Psychological Science in the Public Interest*, 22(3), 110–161. <https://doi.org/10.1177/15291006211051956>

Gelman, A., & Unwin, A. (2013). Infovis and Statistical Graphics: Different Goals, Different Looks. *Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics*, 22(1), 2–28. <https://doi.org/10.1080/10618600.2012.761137> **Recommended**
